summary: For ages 5–6, teach children to name and locate the basic parts of a flowering plant (roots, stem, leaves, flower) and of a tree (roots, trunk, branches, leaves), and to see that a tree shares the same body plan as a small plant — a trunk is a woody stem. Ground the work in real plants and labelled drawings, give deliberate attention to the hidden roots, and introduce function only lightly (roots take in water, leaves catch sunlight).
misconceptions: Omitting or forgetting the roots because they are hidden underground — 'the plant starts at the soil'.
Not recognising a tree as a plant with the same basic parts (trunk = woody stem).
Thinking the stem is just a 'stick' with no role, or that leaves are only for looks.
Confusing flower and fruit, or believing all plants have showy flowers.

activities.title: Pull up a real plant and draw a labelled diagram
steps: Observe a real flowering potted plant, then a small flowering weed or plant that has been pulled up so the roots are visible, rinsing soil off so the root system shows.
Point to and name each part out loud: roots, stem, leaves, flower.
Draw the whole plant from observation, including the roots below a soil line, and write or copy a label on each part.
Discuss which part is normally hidden and would be easy to forget (the roots).
activities.insight: A flowering plant has roots, stem, leaves and a flower; the roots are a real part of the plant even though they are usually hidden underground.

activities.title: Soil cross-section picture: reveal parts and dig down to the roots
steps: Look at a picture of a flowering plant growing in a cut-away slice of ground, so the roots are shown spreading below the surface.
Tap or point to each part to reveal its name and a one-line job: the leaves catch a beam of sunlight; the flower 'makes seeds for new plants'.
Tap or 'dig down' to the roots beneath the soil line and watch them take in water that travels up into the stem.
Say back which part is under the ground and which part catches the sunlight.
activities.insight: Every part of the plant, including the underground roots, has a place and a simple job; roots take in water and leaves catch sunlight.

activities.title: Map the tree onto the little plant
steps: Look at a small flowering plant and a tree side by side.
Match equivalent parts: the tree's trunk to the plant's stem, the tree's branches to stems, and the leaves and roots on both.
Say in your own words why a tree is a plant too, highlighting the trunk as 'a big woody stem'.
Name the tree parts: roots, trunk, branches, leaves.
activities.insight: A tree has the same basic body plan as a small flowering plant — the trunk is a woody stem and branches are stems — so a tree is a big, woody plant.

activities.title: Build the plant from a parts tray
steps: From a tray of part cards (roots, stem, leaves, flower), place each part in its correct position to assemble a whole plant.
Do the same for a tree (roots, trunk, branches, leaves).
Self-check: a misplaced part is returned so the child can try again.
After building, name each part placed.
activities.insight: The parts belong together as one organised plant, each in its own place; a small flowering plant and a tree are built from the same basic kinds of parts — roots, a stem (a woody trunk with branches on the tree) and leaves.

activities.title: Check: label the parts and say the root's job
steps: On a diagram of a whole plant with roots showing, point to and name the roots, stem, leaves and flower.
On a picture of a tree, point to and name the roots, trunk, branches and leaves.
Match each tree part to its flowering-plant equivalent.
Answer aloud: what is the job of the roots — what are they doing down in the soil? Which part catches the sunlight?
activities.insight: Secure naming and locating of parts on both a plant and a tree, tied to the first functions: roots take in water (and hold the plant steady) and leaves catch sunlight.

checkQuestion: Here's a picture of a whole plant with its roots showing, and a picture of a big tree. Point to the roots, stem, leaves and flower on the plant, and the roots, trunk, branches and leaves on the tree. Then tell me: what is the job of the roots — what are they doing down in the soil?
checkAnswer: Correctly points to and names roots, stem, leaves, flower (and tree: roots, trunk, branches, leaves). Says the roots take in WATER (and hold the plant steady in the ground). Full marks pair correct labelling with roots doing water uptake, not just 'holding on'.
